query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A well‐controlled post-solidification annealing treatment that promotes targeted solute segregation to the lamellar interfaces reduces dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations, thereby enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even increasing the alloy’s high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure that exhibits high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.intervention: A single, optimized annealing step performed after solidification under an inert atmosphere at a temperature and duration that induce controlled diffusion of one or more solute elements toward the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: The annealing should be executed under conditions that modify the lamellar boundary chemistry without causing significant coarsening of the primary phases, and the resulting alloy should be tested under standard room-temperature tensile loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, compliant, solute-enriched interfacial layer at the lamellar boundaries that acts as a buffer for dislocation transfer.
generation.mechanism: The controlled annealing treatment drives selective solute segregation to the stiff lamellar boundaries. This localized chemical modification produces a slightly softer interfacial layer, which facilitates smoother dislocation motion, reduces dislocation pile-ups, and diminishes local stress concentrations that typically trigger microcracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy is predicted to display significantly higher tensile ductility (greater elongation at failure) while maintaining or slightly increasing the yield and ultimate tensile strengths during room-temperature tests.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy, which exhibits a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with high intrinsic strength but brittle behavior due to dislocation accumulation at stiff internal interfaces.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under room-temperature tensile conditions; its benefits may be compromised if the annealing parameters lead to excessive grain coarsening or if the solute segregation does not produce a sufficiently compliant interface.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing temperature, time, and choice of segregating solute(s) require optimization, and there is some uncertainty regarding the quantitative improvement in ductility without minute changes in strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA: one group undergoes the proposed annealing treatment while the other serves as the untreated control. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to record stress-strain curves and evaluate yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at failure. Additionally, employ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to inspect the lamellar boundaries for evidence of solute enrichment and to compare dislocation densities and pile-ups between treated and untreated samples.
measurements: Stress-strain curves capturing yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture elongation
TEM imaging of lamellar boundaries to assess the presence and continuity of the solute-enriched interfacial layer, and to quantify dislocation pile-ups
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in ductility (i.e., increased fracture elongation) while retaining comparable or higher strengths compared to the control, or if the expected interfacial solute segregation and reduction in dislocation pile-ups are not observed via TEM, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. frame.system: The starting material is a eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual‐phase lamellar colonies in its as-cast or conventionally processed state, which exhibits high strength but suffers from brittle room-temperature tensile behavior.
frame.goal: To overcome the limited tensile ductility and brittleness at room temperature while retaining or even increasing the alloy’s strength.
frame.limitation: The current microstructure causes dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries that lead to local stress concentrations, subsequent microcracking, and ultimately catastrophic failure during straining.
constraints: A single intervention must be identified
The treatment must preserve or enhance the high strength of the material
The improvement must be effective under room-temperature tensile loading conditions
frame.regime: The primary operating and testing condition is room-temperature tensile deformation, which simulates the service environment where brittleness is critical.
prior_attempts: Prior approaches in similar high-entropy alloy systems have included thermomechanical processing to refine microstructure or dual-phase adjustment; however, these methods did not eliminate the dislocation pile-up issues at the internal boundaries effectively.
Conventional alloying methods and phase refinement techniques have also been used but often at the expense of strength or by requiring multiple interventions.

decision.trend: Early research on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) with dual‐phase lamellar colonies has explored how processing and thermal treatments influence both strength and ductility. For example, the 2014 study (PMC4145285) demonstrated that as‐cast eutectic HEAs featuring a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure could attain high strength and decent ductility, with additional cold processing increasing strength further. Building on this, the 2018 study (PMC5995863) on a refractory HEA showed that a sequence of heat treatments – including solutionizing and long-term annealing – could invert the microstructure, thereby shifting the balance between the hard matrix and softer precipitates to improve ductility. Despite these advances, dislocation pile-up at the internal lamellar boundaries, which induces local stress concentrations and microcracking, remains a persistent issue.
decision.unsolved: The specific challenge of alleviating dislocation pile-ups at the internal lamellar interfaces without compromising (or even enhancing) the high strength remains unsolved. Although stepwise thermo‐mechanical processing has enabled modifications in phase distribution and led to improved overall ductility in some HEAs, no single intervention has been identified that directly tailors the lamellar interfaces to promote smoother dislocation transfer under room-temperature tensile loading.
decision.lever: Implement a targeted post-solidification annealing treatment designed to promote controlled solute segregation at the lamellar interfaces, thereby forming a thin, more compliant interfacial layer that can act as a ‘buffer’ to reduce dislocation pile-ups
decision.why: This approach directly follows the observed trend in which thermo-processing (including cold rolling and annealing) modified the microstructure to improve ductility while retaining strength. By specifically engineering the lamellar boundaries via a controlled annealing step, one can reduce local stress concentrations—addressing the key root-cause cues (dislocation pile-ups and microcracking)—while preserving the high-strength primary phases. This single, well-targeted thermal treatment lever leverages prior successes in thermally induced microstructural inversion and suggests a path toward achieving a more ductile eutectic HEA.
